title: Dynamic Updates in the Domain Name System (DNS UPDATE)
summary: This standards-track specification defines the DNS UPDATE opcode, which lets a client add or delete records in a zone while the server runs. Updates can depend on prerequisites, such as whether a record set already exists.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2136 defines DNS UPDATE, which lets a client add or delete records in a zone while a name server serves it. A request can state what must already be true, and the server makes all requested changes only if every condition holds. Strong access controls are essential because the update message alone does not authenticate or authorize the requester.

questions: how to add records to a dns zone dynamically
how does dynamic dns update work
subtitle: A DNS message for making conditional, all-or-nothing changes to a zone while it is served.

tldr.problem: DNS zones were usually changed by editing a zone file outside the running server. Clients needed a way to add and remove records while the zone remained available.
tldr.mechanism: The UPDATE opcode names one zone, states prerequisites about its current records, and lists changes to apply. The primary master applies the update only if the prerequisites pass, and the transaction is atomic.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2136 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1035 and has itself been updated by RFC 3007, RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035. Without RFC 2137 or equivalent security, anyone who can reach an authoritative server could change its zones.

today: RFC 2136 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1035. It has been updated by RFC 3007, RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

sections.title: Changing a DNS Zone While It Is Served
sections.content:
DNS was designed around a database that changed infrequently, with administrators editing a zone's Master File from outside the running service. RFC 2136 defines the UPDATE opcode so a client can add or delete resource records (RRs) and record sets (RRsets) in a specified zone while it is being served.

The primary master is the authoritative master at the root of the zone-transfer dependency graph, named in the zone's SOA MNAME field. Only that server modifies the zone; a slave forwards an update toward it. The RFC also defines how names and records are compared, with wildcards and aliases disabled during updates.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS UPDATE lets a client request record changes without editing the zone file directly. The primary master makes those changes, while other authoritative servers can forward the request to it.

sections.title: The Five Parts of an UPDATE Message
sections.content:
An UPDATE message has a Header, Zone section, Prerequisite section, Update section and Additional Data section. The Zone section identifies the one zone being changed; the Prerequisite section describes conditions on its current contents; and the Update section lists additions or deletions. Additional Data can carry related information such as glue records.

The Zone section contains exactly one record, with SOA as its type. The opcode value for UPDATE is 5. The message may use UDP if it fits in one datagram, or TCP. Special CLASS values mark deletion and prerequisite operations, and the RFC assigns response codes for update-specific failures.
sections.plainLanguage: An UPDATE request identifies a zone, states what must be true, and lists the records to add or delete. The server uses the special section and class values to interpret those instructions.

sections.title: Prerequisites for a Safe Change
sections.content:
The Prerequisite section can require that a name or RRset exists, does not exist, or matches a specific set of records. These conditions are checked against the zone when the primary master receives the request. An RRset is a set of records with the same name, class and type.

The request can therefore say, for example, that a record set must not already exist before adding it, or that its current values must match before replacing them. If any prerequisite fails, the server performs none of the requested update operations and returns an error code describing the failure.
sections.plainLanguage: Prerequisites let a client describe the zone state that must exist before a change is safe. If even one condition fails, the server makes none of the requested changes.

sections.title: Checking and Applying an Update
sections.content:
The server first checks that the request names one zone and that it is authoritative for that zone. A slave forwards the request; the primary master checks every prerequisite and then checks the requestor's permission. The permission mechanism is implementation-dependent in this specification.

If the checks pass, the primary master processes the Update section in order. It can add records, delete an RRset, delete all RRsets from a name, or delete one record from a set. Duplicate additions and attempts to delete absent data are ignored. The transaction is atomic, and the server must commit changes to nonvolatile storage before responding or serving the changed zone.

If an update does not change the SOA serial, the server increments it automatically before the change is made visible. The RFC suggests a configurable update-count trigger whose default is one hundred updates.
sections.plainLanguage: The primary master checks authority, conditions and permission before processing the change list. It applies the transaction as a whole and saves the result before reporting success or serving the changed zone.

sections.title: Retries, Duplicate Requests and Forwarding
sections.content:
A request or response may be lost, duplicated or delivered out of order. For duplicate protection, the RFC describes a marker record: the request requires an old marker value, then deletes it and adds a different value. Once one copy succeeds, a duplicate no longer meets the prerequisite.

A lost UDP response can make a successful update appear to have failed when a retry encounters changed prerequisites. The RFC therefore says requestors that need an accurate response code must use TCP. A slave forwarding an update allocates a new message identifier, sends it toward its configured transfer source, and waits for that server's response before replying to the client.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks can lose or repeat update messages, so a client can use a prerequisite marker to prevent the same change from succeeding twice. TCP avoids ambiguity about a lost UDP response when the client needs to know the result.

sections.title: Operational Limits and Design Notes
sections.content:
The RFC's design notes say that all data-present and data-absent conditions should be expressed as prerequisites. The protocol cannot create a zone, and adding or deleting the zone's SOA is unsupported. A server is not required to check whether an added record makes semantic sense.

Without a secure update protocol, servers are expected to restrict updates to statically configured source addresses. The RFC names DHCP servers as likely candidates for such a list. It also warns that UPDATE forwarding follows the zone-transfer dependency graph, which must not contain loops because UPDATE has no loop-detection mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: UPDATE changes records in an existing zone but does not create zones or validate every new record's meaning. Without a secure update mechanism, the RFC expects servers to limit which source addresses may submit changes.

sections.title: Security Risks of Unauthorized Updates
sections.content:
Without RFC 2137 or equivalent protection, anyone who can reach an authoritative name server could change any zone on that server. RFC 2136 describes this as a serious increase in vulnerability and very strongly recommends not using UPDATE without equivalent security measures, such as IPsec.

The RFC also describes a denial-of-service risk: an attacker can open TCP sessions to a forwarder and submit changes that the primary master later refuses. The forwarding server's synchronous connections can tie up resources, so some queries may go unanswered during the attack.
sections.plainLanguage: The UPDATE format does not prove who sent a request or whether they may change the zone. The RFC strongly recommends adding strong security, because an exposed server could otherwise accept unauthorized changes.

viz.caption: CONDITIONS THAT CAN BE CHECKED BEFORE AN UPDATE

items.label: YXDOMAIN
items.desc: A name that should not exist does exist.

items.label: YXRRSET
items.desc: An RRset that should not exist does exist.

items.label: NXRRSET
items.desc: An RRset that should exist does not exist.

items.label: NOTAUTH
items.desc: The server is not authoritative for the zone.

items.label: NOTZONE
items.desc: A name in the request is outside the zone.
